title: Who took part
text: The IP-PAD UK data combine four online surveys with 4,968 interviews in total, two waves each by Gallup International and Survation. The surveys reached different age groups in different ways, which matters for every comparison in the other insights.

title: Who took part
section: Two ways of reaching young people
text:
Two ways of reaching young people
Gallup International interviewed panel members aged 16 and over, who answered every question themselves. Survation reached children through their parents, who gave consent and reported the child’s age, gender, region and type of place before handing the device to the child. In the Survation surveys, these background details thus come from parents, while the questions on politics and household income were answered by the young people themselves.

title: Who took part
text:
Age

Each panel shows one survey. The bars give the number of respondents at each year of age, on a shared age axis from 12 to 26.










Survation W1 covers ages 12 to 17 and Survation W2 ages 12 to 18, with a median age of 15 in both. Gallup W1 covers ages 16 to 21, while Gallup W2, which added a separate sample of young adults, spans ages 16 to 26 with a median of 21. The providers thus overlap only at ages 16 to 18, and even there the numbers are uneven. Gallup has 167 respondents aged 16 or 17 in W1 and 121 in W2, and Survation W2 has only 25 respondents aged 18. Gallup W2 also has 332 respondents aged 25, against at most 239 at any other age, a peak that the fieldwork documents do not explain.

title: Who took part
text:
When the surveys took place

Each row is one survey. The height of a bar shows the share of that survey’s interviews carried out in a given month. The dashed line marks the general election of 4 July 2024.










The wave number does not order the surveys in time. Gallup W1 was fielded in May and June 2024, during the general election campaign and under a Conservative government. Survation W1 followed in the summer of 2025. Gallup W2 started in May 2025, but 95% of its interviews took place in November and December 2025, and Survation W2 ran in the autumn of 2026. All surveys but the first thus took place under a Labour government, and differences between them can reflect the time of fieldwork as well as the age of the respondents.

title: Who took part
text:
Gender, place, education and income

Each row is one answer, grouped by question. The dots show the share of respondents in each survey who gave that answer.










In gender and place, the four samples look much alike. Between 48% and 51% of respondents in each survey are female, and 24 in total describe their gender in another way. Most live in a large town or city, from 44% in Survation W2 to 62% in Survation W1, and every UK region is represented. Education, however, mostly follows age, because it combines the level that respondents are studying for with the highest level attained by those who have left education. In the Survation surveys, 72% are in the lowest group (ISCED 0 to 2), mainly because most are still working towards their GCSEs. In Gallup, by contrast, 35% of those aged 18 to 21 and 66% of those aged 22 to 26 are studying for or hold a tertiary qualification (ISCED 5 to 8).
Household income shows a less expected pattern. In both Gallup surveys, 38% say that their household is living comfortably on its present income. In Survation W1 this share is 52%, but in Survation W2 it is only 30%, although both surveys used the same design. Young adolescents may find this question hard to judge, and the gap could also reflect who took part, so we would not read it as a change in household finances.

title: Who took part
text:
Fresh and recontacted respondents
Both second waves first invited earlier respondents back, but only 55 returned to Gallup W2 (5.6% of Gallup W1) and 72 to Survation W2 (7.3% of Survation W1). The data thus come from 4,841 different young people, and each survey is best treated as a separate snapshot rather than as a panel.
The samples are not weighted, so the shares on this page describe the respondents rather than all young people in the UK. The data page describes how the surveys were designed.

title: The same young people a year later
text: Comparing young people of different ages says little about how the views of any one person develop. Both providers therefore re-interviewed some of their respondents. Gallup interviewed 55 young people first in May 2024 and again in 2025, and Survation interviewed 72 in August 2025 and again in September 2026. We ask how much their answers changed on average and how stable they were from one person to the next.

title: The same young people a year later
text:
How certain the links are
Because the interviews were more than a year apart, a correctly linked respondent should be one or two years older in the second wave and report the same gender. Survation’s documented rule, which also accepts an unchanged age, is met by 52 of 55 Gallup links and 60 of 72 Survation links. A stricter rule requiring an age one or two years higher is met by only 48 and 39 links. Since Survation reached children through a parent’s panel account, a sibling may have answered some second interviews. We therefore show each result for all links and, as a check, for the strict links only.

title: The same young people a year later
text:
Average change is small

Each dot is the average change from the first to the second wave, with a line for its 95% confidence interval, and open circles repeat it for the strict links only. To compare measures, all are expressed in points of a scale from 0 to 10. Survation did not ask about trust or the progressive-conservative scale in its second wave.










On most measures, the average answers barely moved. The clearest change is that the Gallup panel felt less warmly about the Labour Party, by 1.1 points (95% interval of the change −1.8 to −0.4) on the scale from 0 to 10, and this holds for the strict links. As the general election of July 2024 fell between the two Gallup waves, this could reflect Labour’s move from opposition into government rather than anything specific to young people. In the Survation panel, feelings about Labour rose by 0.64 points (95% interval of the change 0.02 to 1.25) and certainty about one’s own beliefs fell by 4.4 points (95% interval of the change −8.5 to −0.3) on a scale from 0 to 100, but neither change is clear with the strict links only.

title: The same young people a year later
section: Individual answers move more than the averages
text:
Individual answers move more than the averages

The bars show how many young people moved by a given number of points on the left-right scale. The shaded band marks a change of at most one point.










Behind these small averages, individuals move in both directions. On the left-right scale, 53% of the Gallup panel and 54% of the Survation panel chose the same point twice, but 18% of the Survation panel moved by three points or more. Those who started near the ends of the scale tended to move towards the centre. The 11 Survation respondents who first placed themselves at 3 or below moved right by 2.0 points on average, and the 12 who started at 7 or above moved left by 2.2. Measurement error alone would produce this pattern, because an answer that is extreme partly by chance tends to be less extreme the next time. It therefore need not mean that these young people became more moderate.

title: The same young people a year later
text:
How stable answers are

Each dot is the correlation between the answers in the two waves. A value of 1 means that everyone kept their position relative to the others, and 0 that the first answer says nothing about the second. Open circles show the strict links only.










Most correlations between the waves lie between 0.5 and 0.7, so young people largely keep their position relative to each other even though single answers vary. Left-right self-placement is the most stable measure in Gallup (0.80) but the least stable in Survation (0.42, or 0.48 with the strict links only). This could reflect that many of the 12 to 17 year olds in Survation do not yet have a settled sense of what left and right mean.
The panels are small, include only those who agreed to take part again and may contain some wrong links, so only large changes can be detected with confidence, and none of them tells us why views changed. The data page describes the panel links and how the surveys differ.

title: Views on the economy, morality, climate and immigration
text: Young people who call themselves left or right can still disagree on concrete questions. All four surveys therefore asked how far respondents agree with fourteen statements on the economy, moral questions, climate change and immigration, with the option to say that they did not know. Agreeing expresses a progressive view for some statements and a conservative one for others, which helps to tell genuine views apart from a general tendency to agree.

title: Views on the economy, morality, climate and immigration
section: Broad agreement, with more division on welfare and immigration
text:
Broad agreement, with more division on welfare and immigration

Each bar shows the answers to one statement, with disagreement to the left and agreement to the right of the centre line. Neutral answers are split evenly across it, and the narrow column gives the share who did not know. All four surveys are pooled.










On moral questions and climate change, clear majorities take the progressive side. About two thirds agree that one parent can raise a child as well as two (67%) and that terminally ill people should have a right to assisted dying (69%), while the opposite statements on discrimination against women and climate change find more disagreement than agreement. On the economy, however, answers fit less neatly into one position. Most agree that the government should reduce income differences (68%), yet 51% also accept large differences as a reward for talent and effort, and slightly more agree than disagree that welfare benefits make people lazy. These patterns hold within each survey.
Immigration divides young people most, and the surveys also differ most on it. In Survation W2, 47% agree that immigration makes the UK a worse place to live, compared with 34% in Survation W1 a year earlier, although both cover the same ages. This could reflect change over time, but also differences in who took part or in question order, as Survation W2 asked these statements after an experiment on ideology.

title: Views on the economy, morality, climate and immigration
section: Gender gaps are largest on questions about gender and family
text:
Gender gaps are largest on questions about gender and family

Each row compares the share of young women and young men who agree with a statement in one survey. A longer line means a larger gap.










Young women more often than young men agree that one parent can raise a child as well as two, with gaps of between 6 and 16 percentage points, and less often that discrimination against women is no longer a problem. These gaps are larger in Gallup than among the 12 to 17 year olds in Survation, whose gender was reported by a parent. On climate change, only Gallup shows a gap, with young men more often seeing its impact as exaggerated.

title: Views on the economy, morality, climate and immigration
section: Older respondents agree more, on both sides
text:
Older respondents agree more, on both sides

Each panel shows one statement in Gallup W2, with the share who agree in each age group and a line for the 95% confidence interval. The lower row holds the counterparts of the statements in the upper row.










Because the surveys cover different ages, we look at age within Gallup W2, the only survey that spans ages 16 to 26. There, older respondents agree more often with statements on both sides of the same issue. Agreement that the government should reduce income differences rises from 62% among 16 and 17 year olds to 71% among 22 to 26 year olds, but agreement that large income differences are acceptable also rises, from 37% to 54%. If anything, older respondents seem more willing to agree in general rather than more left or right. Differences in who took part at each age could also play a role, and only 121 respondents are aged 16 or 17.

title: Views on the economy, morality, climate and immigration
text:
Few answer “I don’t know”

Each dot is the share of “I don’t know” answers across all fourteen statements, at one year of age in one survey. Ages with fewer than 20 respondents are left out.










Only 3% of all answers are “I don’t know”. In Survation, 12 to 14 year olds choose it somewhat more often (5% of their answers) than 15 to 17 year olds (3%), most of all on assisted dying. Gallup W2 has the fewest such answers at every age, so the differences between surveys are as large as those between ages.
The overview pools all interviews without weights, so Gallup W2, which is twice as large as the other surveys, counts twice as much there. Gallup W1 also shows signs of weaker response quality on the immigration statements, but leaving it out changes no pooled share of agreement by more than 2 percentage points. The data page describes how the surveys differ.

title: Explore the data
About
text:
IP-PAD, short for Interdisciplinary Perspectives on the Politics of Adolescence and Democracy, is a Doctoral Network funded by the European Union under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions. It studies how the cognitive, emotional and social changes of adolescence and early adulthood shape the way young people process political information and engage with politics.
As part of this work, the network surveys young people in Austria, Greece, the Netherlands, Poland and the United Kingdom, using a common set of questions and inviting respondents back in later waves. This website presents the UK data, which were collected by the team at Royal Holloway, University of London, with fieldwork by Gallup International and Survation. The data page describes how the surveys were carried out.

title: The data
text: The IP-PAD UK data combine four online surveys of young people in the United Kingdom, carried out between 2024 and 2026 by two fieldwork providers that each ran two waves. The combined file has one row per interview and holds 4,968 interviews with 4,841 young people. Apart from two questions about the future that only Survation asked, it includes only questions asked in at least two of the surveys.

Gallup respondents answered all questions themselves. In the Survation surveys, a parent first gave consent and reported the child’s age, gender, region and type of place, before the child answered the rest of the questionnaire. In both second waves, the providers invited their first-wave respondents back and then added new respondents. Because few Gallup respondents returned, Gallup W2 added a separate sample of 22 to 26 year olds, and Survation W2 also admitted 25 respondents aged 18 outside its quota.

title: The data
section: When the surveys were in the field
text:
When the surveys were in the field

Each row shows one survey. The bars give the number of interviews in each month, on the same scale for all four surveys.










Three of the surveys carried out most of their interviews within two or three months. Gallup W2 began in May 2025 with a few interviews each month, and 95% of its interviews took place in November and December 2025, when the 22 to 26 year olds were added.

title: The data
text:
Before comparing surveys
The four surveys share most of their questions but were not designed as one sample. The differences below matter whenever answers are compared across surveys, and the explorer lets you check whether a pattern holds in each survey separately.

Different age ranges. The two providers overlap only at ages 16 to 18, so a difference between Gallup and Survation can reflect age as much as the provider.
Wave is not time. The variable wave counts the waves within each provider. Survation W1 was in the field in the summer of 2025, while Gallup W2 was still running, so the fieldwork dates are the better guide to timing.
Not weighted. All respondents come from online panels and the data are not weighted, so the results describe the young people who took part rather than all young people in the UK.
Different quality checks. Each survey removed careless or automated answers by its own rules. Gallup W1, for example, kept respondents who failed its attention check, whereas Survation removed those who failed two checks.
Survation W1 scores higher on 0 to 10 scales. Averaged over the five party ratings and the left-right scale, Survation W1 respondents score 5.4, against 4.3 to 4.5 in the other surveys. Those who took part again a year later had already answered much like the other surveys in the first wave (4.3), which suggests that the difference lies in who took part. The insight on left and right shows an example.
Few and uncertain panel links. Only 55 Gallup and 72 Survation respondents took part in both waves of their provider. Judged by age and gender, 48 of the Gallup links and 39 of the Survation links are plausible. Survation links run through the parent’s panel account, so a sibling may have answered in some cases.
Small wording differences. A few questions were worded slightly differently between the surveys, such as the introduction to the party ratings. The codebook notes each of these differences.

title: How young people in the UK think about politics
text:
Interdisciplinary Perspectives on the Politics of Adolescence and Democracy




Between 2024 and 2026, we surveyed young people across the United Kingdom about politics, from 12-year-olds to young adults in their mid twenties. On this site, we describe the samples and provide interactive insights into the data.




4


surveys, two run by Gallup International and two by Survation




4,968


interviews with 4,841 young people




12 to 26


years of age, with those under 18 recruited through their parents




127


young people took part in both waves of a survey
Two fieldwork providers carried out the surveys for us. Gallup International interviewed 16 to 26 year olds from its online panels, and Survation reached 12 to 18 year olds through their parents. Each provider ran two waves about a year apart and invited the first-wave respondents back for the second, which is why some young people answered our questions twice.

title: Interest, democracy and trust
text: Attitudes towards politics and democracy that form in adolescence and early adulthood can last into later life. All four surveys asked about political interest and satisfaction with democracy, and three asked about trust in five institutions. Because the surveys cover different ages, we mostly compare age groups within a survey.

title: Interest, democracy and trust
text:
Interest in politics

Each line shows one survey. The dots give the share of respondents at each year of age who are fairly or very interested in politics. Ages with fewer than 20 respondents in a survey are left out.










In Gallup W2, the only survey that covers ages 16 to 26, the share fairly or very interested in politics rises from 38% at age 16 to 75% at age 26. Gallup W1 shows a similar rise between 16 and 21. In Survation, by contrast, interest varies less between ages 12 and 17. The two Survation waves also differ, with 57% fairly or very interested in W1 but only 43% in W2. However, the 72 Survation W1 respondents who took part again a year later were less interested in W1 (39%) than the others (59%), which suggests that the gap partly reflects who took part. Within each survey, young men report interest in politics slightly more often than young women, by 4 to 6 percentage points.

title: Interest, democracy and trust
text:
Satisfaction with democracy

Each bar shows the answers of young women or young men in one survey to the statement “I am satisfied with the way that democracy works in the United Kingdom”, on a scale from 1 (fully disagree) to 7 (fully agree).










In both Gallup surveys, more young people are dissatisfied than satisfied with how democracy works in the UK (48% against 30% in W1, and 45% against 33% in W2). Among the adolescents in Survation, more are satisfied than dissatisfied in W1, while in W2 the two groups are of similar size and 35% choose the middle of the scale. In every survey, young women are satisfied less often than young men, for instance 29% against 38% in Gallup W2. Within Gallup W2, satisfaction is also more common among 22 to 26 year olds (40%) than 18 to 21 year olds (27%). Across the surveys, satisfaction goes together with interest, as 56% of those very interested in politics are satisfied, compared with 13% of those not at all interested.

title: Interest, democracy and trust
text:
Trust in institutions

Each row is one institution, and the dots give its average trust rating in each survey on a scale from 0 (no trust at all) to 10 (complete trust). Survation W2 did not ask these questions.










In every survey that asked about trust, the courts and the police are trusted most and political parties and the media least. In Gallup W1, for example, trust averages 4.9 for the police but 3.7 for political parties. Survation W1 shows higher trust in every institution, which fits its higher answers on all 0 to 10 scales. Gallup W1 was fielded under a Conservative government and Gallup W2 under a Labour one, yet among 18 to 21 year olds, the one age group both surveys cover well, trust in the UK government is almost the same (3.7 and 3.9). The higher Gallup W2 average thus comes mainly from its 22 to 26 year olds (5.0). In both Gallup surveys, young men trust the government somewhat more than young women, for instance 4.7 against 4.2 in Gallup W2.

title: Interest, democracy and trust
text:
Ways of governing

Each row is one way of governing a country. The dots give the share of respondents in each survey who find it fairly or very good (5 to 7 on a scale from 1, very bad, to 7, very good).










Large majorities in all surveys find democratic ways of governing good, and elections where every vote counts equally receive the most support, from 69% in Gallup W1 to 90% in Survation W1. At the same time, a strong leader who accepts no interference is rated good by 40% in Gallup W1, 48% in Gallup W2 and close to three fifths in both Survation surveys. These views can coexist, as 52% of Survation W2 respondents rate both equal elections and a strong leader as good. Some may read “strong leader” as effective leadership rather than a rejection of democratic checks, but these data cannot tell.
The samples are not weighted and the surveys differ in age range and recruitment, so differences between them should be read with care. The data page describes how the surveys differ.

title: Left, right and the centre
text: Left and right remain the most common shorthand for political positions, but it is not obvious that young people, and adolescents in particular, think about politics in these terms. In all four surveys, respondents placed themselves on a scale from 0 (left) to 10 (right), and we look at how their answers differ with age and between young women and young men.

title: Left, right and the centre
section: Most answers are close to the centre
text:
Most answers are close to the centre

Each panel shows one survey. The bars give the share of respondents who chose each point of the scale.










Across the four surveys, 49% of respondents placed themselves between 4 and 6, and the exact middle was by far the most common answer. This was particularly true of the youngest respondents. Among those aged 12 to 15, 38% chose the midpoint, compared with 29% among those aged 18 and over. For some, the middle will reflect a genuinely moderate position. For others, it may indicate that they do not (yet) think about politics in terms of left and right, so averages on this scale should be read with care.
The average positions in Gallup W1 (4.4), Gallup W2 (5.0) and Survation W2 (5.0) are close to each other, whereas Survation W1 stands out at 6.1. We do not think this reflects a real shift to the right among younger adolescents. Respondents in Survation W1 gave higher answers on all scales from 0 to 10, and those who took part again a year later placed themselves much like respondents in the other surveys. The difference thus seems to come from who took part rather than from what young people of that age think (see The data).

title: Left, right and the centre
text:
Age

Each dot is the average position at one year of age in one survey, with a line for its 95% confidence interval. Ages with fewer than 20 respondents in a survey are left out.










Within Gallup W1 and the two Survation surveys, the average position hardly changes with age. The clearest pattern appears in Gallup W2, the only survey that covers the full range from 16 to 26, where the average rises from 4.0 among 16 and 17 year olds to 4.5 among 18 to 21 year olds and 5.5 among those aged 22 to 26. A single survey cannot tell whether this reflects young people moving to the right as they grow older or differences between generations. Because the surveys cover different age ranges, a curve drawn across all ages from 12 to 26 would also mix differences between ages with differences between surveys.

title: Left, right and the centre
text:
Gender

Each row compares the average position of young women and young men in one age group of one survey. A longer line means a larger gap. Groups with fewer than 20 respondents are left out.










The gender difference is the most consistent pattern in these data. In every survey and age group, young women place themselves further left than young men. However, the size of the gap changes with age. Pooled over the surveys, it is only 0.2 points among 12 to 15 year olds, but grows to 0.6 points among 16 and 17 year olds and 0.8 points among 18 to 21 year olds, before narrowing slightly to 0.5 points among those aged 22 to 26. The gap thus seems to open up in the late teens, a period that research on political socialisation regards as formative for political attitudes.

title: Left, right and the centre
section: Left and right, progressive and conservative
text:
Left and right, progressive and conservative
Three of the four surveys also asked respondents to place themselves between socially progressive (0) and socially conservative (10). The two scales correlate at 0.48, so young people who see themselves on the left also tend to describe themselves as progressive. However, the relationship is far from perfect, which suggests that for many young people social values and left-right position do not fully coincide. You can compare both scales by age, gender and survey in the explorer.
The samples are not weighted and the surveys differ in age range and recruitment, so we compare groups within the same survey where possible. The data page describes how the surveys differ.

title: Feelings towards the parties
text: Most respondents are too young to vote, so their feelings towards the parties are one of the few ways to see how they relate to party politics. All four surveys asked them to rate five parties from 0 (strongly dislike) to 10 (strongly like). Gallup W1 was fielded during the 2024 general election campaign, under a Conservative government, while all later surveys took place after Labour had come to power (see Who took part).

title: Feelings towards the parties
text:
Which parties young people like

Each panel shows one survey. Bars to the right give the share of respondents who rate a party 7 or higher, bars to the left the share who rate it 3 or lower. Ratings of 4 to 6 are not shown.










Labour is liked by the largest share of respondents in Gallup W1 (33%) and in both Survation surveys. Gallup W2 is the exception, where 33% like the Greens and 29% like Labour. The Conservatives and Reform UK are disliked most often. In Gallup W1, 53% rate the Conservatives 3 or lower, and in both second waves Reform UK receives a rating of 0 more often than any other party (28% in Gallup W2, 28% in Survation W2). Yet 25% of Survation W2 respondents like Reform UK, about as many as like the Greens, which suggests that Reform UK divides young people more sharply than other parties.
Survation W1 stands apart. Its respondents like every party more often and dislike every party less often, with an average rating of 5.2 across all five parties, against 4.2 to 4.4 in the other surveys. This fits their tendency to give higher answers on 0 to 10 scales, so the order of the parties within this survey is a safer guide than their levels.

title: Feelings towards the parties
text:
Age

Each panel shows one party. The dots give the average rating in each age group of a survey. Groups with fewer than 50 respondents are left out.










Because the surveys cover different age ranges, age differences are best read within a survey. In Gallup W2, 22 to 26 year olds rate the Conservatives at 4.5 on average, against 3.5 among 18 to 21 year olds, and Reform UK at 4.6 against 3.3. They also rate Labour higher, while ratings of the Greens hardly differ by age. As the older group rates almost every party more warmly, this could partly reflect a general tendency to rate higher rather than a preference for particular parties. In the Survation surveys the pattern runs the other way, as 16 and 17 year olds rate all five parties slightly lower than 12 to 15 year olds.

title: Feelings towards the parties
text:
Gender

Each row compares the average rating of a party among young women and young men in one survey. A longer line means a larger gap.










In all four surveys, young men rate the Conservatives higher than young women, by 0.2 to 0.8 points, and Reform UK by 0.1 to 0.8 points. In turn, young women in the two Gallup surveys rate the Greens higher, by 0.3 points in W1 and 0.6 points in W2. The gaps for Labour and the Liberal Democrats are smaller and less consistent, and in Survation W1 young men rate every party somewhat higher.

title: Feelings towards the parties
section: The same ages in two waves
text:
The same ages in two waves

Both panels compare Gallup respondents aged 18 to 21 in W1 (spring 2024, light blue) and W2 (mostly late 2025, dark blue). A longer line means a larger difference between the two surveys.










The Gallup surveys allow a fairer comparison over time, as both include over 800 respondents aged 18 to 21 (821 and 878) recruited in the same way. In this age group, the share who like Labour falls from 33% in W1 to 22% in W2, while the share who like the Greens rises from 23% to 33%. The share who like Reform UK hardly changes, but the share who rate it 0 rises from 17% to 34%. The two surveys lie on either side of the change of government. However, they consist of different young people, so the data cannot tell whether the differences reflect the events of that period or who happened to take part.
Gallup W1 also introduced the parties with slightly different wording, so small differences between surveys should be read with care. The data page describes how the surveys differ.
